q: Which is the largest country in the world by area?
fact: Russia covers about 17 million square km - roughly one ninth of all the land on Earth.

q: Which is the smallest country in the world by area?
fact: Vatican City covers less than half a square km - smaller than many city parks - and lies entirely inside Rome.

q: Which country reports more islands than any other - about 267,000 in its official count?
fact: Fewer than 1,000 of Sweden's islands are inhabited. Stockholm alone is spread across 14 of them.

q: Which country has the longest coastline in the world?
fact: Canada's coast runs for about 202,000 km. Walking it without a single break would take more than four years.

q: Which country is 'doubly landlocked' - surrounded entirely by other landlocked countries?
fact: Only two countries qualify: Uzbekistan and tiny Liechtenstein. Reaching the sea from either means crossing at least two borders.

q: Which is the most populous landlocked country in the world?
fact: Ethiopia has well over 100 million people. It lost its coastline when Eritrea became independent in 1993.

q: Which is the largest landlocked country in the world by area?
fact: Kazakhstan is the ninth-largest country overall. Its only shore is on the Caspian Sea, which has no outlet to the ocean.

q: Which is the only country whose national flag does not have four sides?
fact: Nepal's flag is made of two stacked pennants. Its exact shape is laid out step by step in the constitution.

q: Which is the only country whose national flag has a different emblem on its front and back?
fact: Paraguay's flag shows the national coat of arms on the front and the treasury seal, with a lion, on the back.

q: Which country has been the world's largest coffee producer for more than 150 years?
fact: Brazil grows roughly a third of the world's coffee, far ahead of second-placed Vietnam.

q: Which country grows the most cocoa beans, the raw material of chocolate?
fact: Ivory Coast supplies around 40% of the world's cocoa, most of it grown on small family farms.

q: Which country has more ancient pyramids than any other - roughly twice as many as Egypt?
fact: The Kushite kings of Nubia built more than 200 steep, narrow pyramids, many of them at Meroe.

q: Which country has the most lakes in the world?
fact: By one global survey, about 60% of all the world's lakes larger than ten hectares lie in Canada.

q: Which country is the world's longest and narrowest, stretching about 4,300 km but averaging under 180 km wide?
fact: Chile runs from the Atacama, the driest nonpolar desert on Earth, all the way to glaciers near Antarctica.

q: Which is the lowest-lying country in the world, with natural ground averaging only about 1.5 meters above sea level?
fact: The Maldives is made up of roughly 1,200 coral islands. Its highest natural point is usually put at just 2.4 meters, though some sources say about 5.

q: Which is the only country in the world that lies entirely above 1,000 meters?
fact: Lesotho's lowest point is about 1,400 meters up - the highest low point of any country.

q: Which of these countries is completely surrounded by a single other country?
fact: San Marino sits inside Italy. Vatican City and Lesotho are the only other enclaves like it - Monaco touches only France but also has a sea coast.

q: Which country has the most Spanish speakers in the world?
fact: Mexico has around 130 million people - more than twice the population of Spain.

q: Which country drinks the most tea per person?
fact: People in Turkey get through about 3 kg of tea leaves each per year, usually served black in small tulip-shaped glasses.

q: If every time zone were exactly the same width, how many degrees of longitude would each one cover?
fact: The Earth turns 360 degrees in 24 hours, so one hour on the clock equals 15 degrees of longitude.

q: Which country eats the most chocolate per person?
fact: The Swiss eat roughly 10 kg each per year - and it was a Swiss chocolatier who invented milk chocolate in 1875.

q: Where were the first Winter Olympic Games held, in 1924?
fact: It was staged as an International Winter Sports Week and only later named the first Winter Olympics.

q: Which country has won the most gold medals in the history of the Summer Olympics?
fact: American athletes have won more than 1,000 Summer golds - over twice as many as any other nation.

q: Which country has won the most gold medals in the history of the Winter Olympics?
fact: Norway, with fewer than six million people, owes its lead above all to its cross-country skiers.

q: Which country hosted the first modern Olympic Games in 1896?
fact: The Games in Athens brought together about 240 athletes from 14 nations - all of them men.

q: Which country has the longest written constitution of any nation?
fact: India's constitution runs to about 145,000 words in English. The original was written out by hand in calligraphy.

q: Which country flies the oldest national flag still in use?
fact: According to legend the Dannebrog fell from the sky in 1219. It has been in use since at least the 1300s.

q: Which of these countries has a national anthem with no official words?
fact: Spain's 'Marcha Real' is one of only a handful of wordless anthems. Fans simply hum along at matches.

q: Which is the largest country in the world without a single permanent river?
fact: Saudi Arabia has only wadis, dry valleys that fill briefly after rain. Much of its tap water is desalinated seawater.

q: Which country is hit by more tornadoes than any other?
fact: The United States records over 1,000 tornadoes a year, many of them in the central plains known as Tornado Alley.

q: Which country is home to most of the world's wild tigers?
fact: India's 2022 census counted more than 3,600 wild tigers, well over half of the global total.

q: Which of these countries is more than 90% covered by forest, one of the highest shares in the world?
fact: Rainforest covers almost all of Suriname, one of the few countries that absorb more carbon dioxide than they emit.

q: Which country has the world's highest uninterrupted waterfall, Angel Falls?
fact: The water drops 979 meters from a flat-topped mountain. In the dry season much of it turns to mist before it lands.

q: Which country is the world's largest archipelago nation, with more than 17,000 islands?
fact: Indonesia's islands stretch more than 5,000 km from west to east - wider than the continental United States.

q: Which is the smallest of the world's five oceans?
fact: It is also the shallowest, and much of its surface is covered by sea ice for most of the year.

q: Which country is named after a female saint?
fact: Saint Lucia is named after Saint Lucy of Syracuse. It is often said to be the only country named after a real woman.

q: Which country's name is simply the Spanish word for the line that divides the globe into north and south?
fact: Ecuador means 'equator'. A monument near Quito marks the line, though GPS puts the real one about 240 meters away.

q: Which country's name comes from the Latin word for 'southern'?
fact: Ancient mapmakers imagined a 'Terra Australis', a great southern land. Austria's name, by contrast, means 'eastern realm'.

q: Which is the largest country to use a single time zone for its whole territory?
fact: China spans five geographic time zones but runs entirely on Beijing time, so in the far west the sun can rise at 10 a.m.

q: Which is the largest country located entirely in the Southern Hemisphere?
fact: Brazil is bigger, but the Equator crosses its northern edge. Australia lies wholly south of the line.

q: Which is the most sparsely populated sovereign country in the world?
fact: Mongolia has only about two people per square km - and nearly half of them live in the capital, Ulaanbaatar.

q: Which is the most densely populated sovereign country in the world?
fact: Monaco squeezes nearly 40,000 people into about two square km - an area smaller than New York's Central Park.

q: Which strait separates Asia from North America?
fact: It is about 85 km wide at its narrowest, and the two Diomede Islands in the middle are less than 4 km apart.

q: Which country has the southernmost capital city in the world?
fact: Wellington sits at 41 degrees south and is also known as one of the windiest cities on Earth.

q: Which country gave the Statue of Liberty to the United States as a gift in the 1880s?
fact: The statue crossed the Atlantic in 350 pieces packed into 214 crates. Its iron frame was designed by Gustave Eiffel.

q: In which country did the game of chess originate around 1,500 years ago?
fact: Its ancestor, chaturanga, spread from India to Persia, where 'shah mat' - 'the king is helpless' - became checkmate.

q: Which is the only country whose postage stamps do not carry the country's name?
fact: Britain issued the world's first stamp, the Penny Black, in 1840. Its stamps show the monarch's head instead of a name.

q: Which country has the oldest hereditary monarchy still reigning today?
fact: Japan's imperial line is traditionally traced back to 660 BC, and historians can follow it for at least 1,500 years.

q: Which country produces the most olive oil in the world?
fact: In a normal year Spain makes around 40% of the world's olive oil, most of it in the region of Andalusia.

q: Which country grows about 90% of the world's saffron, the most expensive spice by weight?
fact: Each crocus flower gives just three red threads, picked by hand. A kilogram takes around 150,000 flowers.

q: Which country became the first in the world to ban thin plastic bags, in 2002?
fact: Bangladesh acted after discarded bags were found to be clogging city drains during the monsoon.

q: Which country has the tallest people in the world on average?
fact: Dutch men average about 183 cm and Dutch women about 170 cm.

q: Off which country's coast do the Atlantic and Indian Oceans officially meet?
fact: The two oceans officially meet at Cape Agulhas, the southernmost tip of Africa - not at the more famous Cape of Good Hope.

q: Which country was the first to land a spacecraft on the far side of the Moon, in 2019?
fact: The Chang'e 4 lander needed a relay satellite, because the far side never faces Earth and radio cannot reach it directly.

q: Which country's red-over-white flag is almost identical to Indonesia's, differing mainly in its proportions?
fact: Monaco adopted its flag in 1881, Indonesia in 1945. Poland's flag uses the same two colors the other way up.

q: Which country's blue-yellow-red flag is almost indistinguishable from Romania's?
fact: Chad's blue stripe is officially a slightly darker shade. Andorra and Moldova avoid confusion with a coat of arms.

q: Which country contains the point on Earth's surface that is farthest from the planet's center?
fact: Earth bulges at the Equator, so the summit of Chimborazo is about 2 km farther from the center than the top of Everest.

q: Which symbol appears next to a star on the flags of Turkey, Pakistan and Algeria?
fact: The star and crescent also appears on the flags of Tunisia, Malaysia, Azerbaijan and several other countries.

q: Roughly how much of Earth's entire surface does the Pacific Ocean cover?
fact: The Pacific is larger than all of Earth's land put together and holds about half of its ocean water.

q: What is the largest desert on Earth?
fact: A desert is defined by how little rain or snow falls, not by heat. The Sahara is only the largest hot desert.

q: Which river carries more water to the sea than any other on Earth?
fact: The Amazon delivers about a fifth of all the river water that reaches the world's oceans.

q: Which lake holds about one fifth of all the unfrozen fresh water on Earth's surface?
fact: Baikal in Siberia is also the world's deepest lake, at more than 1,600 meters, and the oldest, at about 25 million years.

q: Despite its name, which body of water is usually counted as the largest lake in the world?
fact: The Caspian is bigger than Germany and is bordered by five countries, from Russia to Iran.

q: Which sea has no coastline at all, bounded only by ocean currents?
fact: It lies in the North Atlantic and is named after the floating sargassum seaweed that gathers there.

q: Roughly how much of Earth's surface is covered by water?
fact: Almost all of it is salty. Only around 3% of Earth's water is fresh, and most of that is locked up in ice.

q: At roughly what latitude do the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn lie?
fact: The number matches the tilt of Earth's axis. The tropics mark the farthest points where the sun can stand directly overhead.

q: What happens to the date when you cross the International Date Line heading west, from America toward Asia?
fact: The line zigzags through the Pacific so that no country is split between two different days.

q: Mount Everest is the highest peak above sea level, but which mountain is tallest from base to summit?
fact: Hawaii's Mauna Kea rises about 10,200 meters from the Pacific seafloor, but more than half of it is underwater.

q: The Ring of Fire, where most of the world's earthquakes and volcanic eruptions occur, circles which ocean?
fact: The horseshoe-shaped belt is about 40,000 km long and holds roughly three quarters of Earth's active volcanoes.

q: What is the largest island in the world that is not a continent?
fact: Greenland is more than three times the size of Texas, and about 80% of it lies under an ice sheet.

q: About how long is the Equator, the full distance around the Earth?
fact: That is no accident: the meter was originally defined so that the distance from the pole to the Equator would be 10,000 km.

q: What do scientists call the ancient supercontinent that held nearly all of Earth's land about 300 million years ago?
fact: The name is Greek for 'all the Earth'. The matching coastlines of Africa and South America are a leftover clue.

q: Which color appears on more national flags than any other?
fact: Red is on roughly three quarters of the world's flags, just ahead of white. Purple is the rarest color.

q: Only two national flags are square. Which countries fly them?
fact: Every other national flag is a rectangle - except Nepal's, which is made of two stacked triangles.

q: What is the study of flags called?
fact: The word was coined in the 1950s from 'vexillum', the cloth banner carried by Roman army units.

q: In flag terminology, what is the 'hoist'?
wrong: The rope that raises the flag
fact: The opposite, free-flying half is called the fly. It wears out first, so designers keep important symbols near the hoist.

q: What does a flag flown at half-mast traditionally signal?
fact: The custom goes back at least to the 1600s, when ships lowered their flags to honor a captain who had died.

q: What do the five rings on the Olympic flag stand for?
fact: Their six colors, counting the white background, were chosen so that every nation's flag shared at least one of them.

q: What is shown in the center of the flag of the United Nations?
answer: A world map inside olive branches
wrong: A dove carrying an olive branch
A globe held by two hands
A circle of twelve gold stars
fact: The map is centered on the North Pole, so no single country sits in the middle of it.

q: How many member states does the United Nations have?
fact: The newest member is South Sudan, which joined in 2011. The Holy See (Vatican City) and Palestine are non-member observer states.

q: How many countries hold a permanent seat on the UN Security Council?
fact: China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States each hold a veto. Ten more members rotate.

q: In which city is the main headquarters of the United Nations?
fact: The site on the East River is international territory. Geneva, Vienna and Nairobi host the UN's other main offices.

q: In which city does the International Court of Justice, the UN's main court, sit?
fact: It works in the Peace Palace, a building paid for by the American steel magnate Andrew Carnegie.

q: Which continent has the most countries?
fact: Africa has 54 member states in the United Nations - more than a quarter of the whole organization.

q: About how many people live on Earth today?
fact: The world passed 8 billion in November 2022 - twice as many people as in 1974.

q: How far from its coast does a country's exclusive economic zone normally extend?
fact: Inside that zone, about 370 km wide, a country controls fishing and seabed resources. Full sovereignty ends at 12 nautical miles.

q: Which UN agency keeps the list of World Heritage Sites?
fact: The list began in 1978 with just 12 sites, including the Galápagos Islands and Yellowstone.

q: Which writing system is used by more people than any other?
fact: By some estimates up to 70% of the world's population uses the Latin alphabet, which the Romans adapted from the Etruscans.

q: Which language has the most native speakers in the world?
fact: Mandarin has over 900 million native speakers. Counting second-language speakers too, English comes out on top.

q: How many official languages does the United Nations work in?
fact: They are Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish. Arabic was the last to be added, in 1973.

q: Roughly how many languages are spoken in the world today?
fact: Over 40% of them are endangered, while about half of the world's people speak just a couple of dozen of them.

q: Which language was invented in 1887 to be an easy second language for the whole world?
fact: Its creator, the Polish eye doctor L. L. Zamenhof, published it under the pen name 'Doktoro Esperanto' - 'Doctor Hopeful'.

q: Which metal are Olympic gold medals mostly made of?
fact: A gold medal must be at least 92.5% silver, plated with about six grams of gold. Solid gold medals ended after 1912.

q: How many teams played in the 2026 FIFA World Cup, the first under the expanded format?
fact: It was also the first World Cup shared by three host countries - Canada, Mexico and the United States - and was won by Spain.

q: In which year was the first FIFA Women's World Cup held?
fact: The tournament took place in China and was won by the United States.

q: What does the traditional Olympic motto 'Citius, Altius, Fortius' mean?
fact: In 2021 a fourth word was officially added to the motto: 'Communiter', meaning 'Together'.

q: In which Swiss city is the International Olympic Committee based?
fact: The IOC moved there from Paris in 1915. Lausanne now calls itself the Olympic Capital and is home to the Olympic Museum.

q: Not counting the Youth Olympics, which inhabited continent has never hosted an Olympic Games?
fact: South America's first Games were in Rio de Janeiro in 2016. Dakar in Senegal hosted the 2026 Youth Olympics, the first Olympic event ever held in Africa.

q: Which of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World is the only one still standing?
fact: It is also the oldest of the seven, built about 4,500 years ago, and was the tallest structure on Earth for some 3,800 years.

q: Who led the first expedition to reach the South Pole, in December 1911?
fact: The Norwegian's team used skis and sled dogs and beat a rival British party to the pole by about five weeks.

q: The first voyage around the world, completed in 1522, set out under which captain?
fact: Magellan died on the way. Only one of his five ships, the Victoria, completed the voyage, under Juan Sebastián Elcano.

q: Which ancient network of trade routes linked China with the Mediterranean?
fact: The name was only coined in 1877 by a German geographer. Paper, spices and ideas traveled along it as well as silk.

q: Which 1959 agreement set aside an entire continent for peace and science?
fact: It bans military bases and weapons tests and puts every territorial claim on the continent on hold.

q: In which year did climbers first reach the summit of Mount Everest?
fact: Edmund Hillary of New Zealand and the Sherpa mountaineer Tenzing Norgay reached the top on May 29.

q: Which grain is the main daily food for more than half of the world's people?
fact: About 90% of the world's rice is both grown and eaten in Asia.

q: After plain water, which drink is consumed more than any other in the world?
fact: People drink billions of cups a day. All true teas - black, green and white - come from the same plant.

q: Potatoes, tomatoes, maize and cacao all originally come from which part of the world?
fact: None of them was known in Europe, Asia or Africa before 1492 - so no tomato sauce in Italy and no chocolate in Switzerland.

q: Which crop is harvested in greater weight than any other in the world?
fact: Around 1.9 billion tons of sugarcane are cut every year, about 40% of it in Brazil.

q: Which currency name is used by more countries than any other?
fact: The word goes back to the 'thaler', a silver coin first minted in the 1500s in the Bohemian valley of Joachimsthal.

q: What do the member countries of the group known as OPEC all export?
fact: OPEC was founded in Baghdad in 1960 by Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela.

q: Roughly what share of the world's traded goods, by volume, travels by sea?
fact: Much of it moves in standard steel containers, an invention of the 1950s that made shipping dramatically cheaper.

q: What does the lighthearted 'Big Mac Index' compare between countries?
fact: The Economist invented it in 1986: if the same burger costs more in one country, its currency may be overvalued.

q: The Prime Meridian, the line of zero degrees longitude, runs through which district of London?
fact: An 1884 conference chose the line through the Royal Observatory. France kept using its own Paris meridian for decades.

q: Which canal links the Mediterranean Sea with the Red Sea?
fact: Opened in 1869, it saves ships sailing between Europe and Asia a detour of thousands of kilometers around Africa.

q: What is the sea route through the Arctic islands north of Canada called?
fact: Explorers searched for it for 400 years. Roald Amundsen finally sailed all the way through in 1903-1906.

q: Which two letters do no countries' English names begin with?
fact: Qatar, Oman and Yemen save Q, O and Y with one country each. Wales starts with W, but it is not a sovereign state.

q: What is the nickname of the spot in the ocean that is farthest from any land?
fact: It lies in the South Pacific about 2,700 km from the nearest shore. Often the closest humans are aboard the Space Station.

q: Which two countries share the longest international land border in the world?
fact: It runs for 8,891 km in two parts, counting Alaska's border. The longest unbroken border, about 7,600 km, lies between Russia and Kazakhstan.
